hints: Remember what cracking does, it splits one long alkane into a smaller alkane plus a smaller alkene.
Check the carbon count first, the carbons in the two products must add up to 17.
Now check hydrogens too, the hydrogens must add to 36, so see which choice would leave an impossible tiny partner like $\text{CH}_2$.
walkthrough:
**Recall what cracking makes**

Cracking breaks a long alkane into a shorter alkane and an alkene. Think of it as snapping one long chain into two useful pieces.

General idea:
$$\text{long alkane} \rightarrow \text{shorter alkane} + \text{alkene}$$

**Use atom balance to test products**

All atoms from $\text{C}_{17}\text{H}_{36}$ must end up in the two products. So carbons must sum to 17 and hydrogens must sum to 36.

Rule to check:
$$C_{product1} + C_{product2} = 17 \text{ and } H_{product1} + H_{product2} = 36$$

**Test the first three choices**

$\text{C}_3\text{H}_8$ is an alkane, so its partner would be $\text{C}_{14}\text{H}_{28}$, a valid alkene. $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ is an alkene, so its partner would be $\text{C}_{13}\text{H}_{28}$, a valid alkane. $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{16}$ is an alkene, so its partner would be $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{20}$, a valid alkane. All of these are sensible cracking splits.

**Spot the impossible split**

$\text{C}_{16}\text{H}_{34}$ is itself an alkane with formula $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$. To make it from $\text{C}_{17}\text{H}_{36}$ you would have only 1 carbon and 2 hydrogens left over.

Impossible balance:
$$\text{C}_{17}\text{H}_{36} \rightarrow \text{C}_{16}\text{H}_{34} + \text{CH}_2$$
$\text{CH}_2$ is not a stable alkane or alkene, so this product is least likely.

options.A: C3H8 is a valid alkane product. Cracking C17H36 could give C3H8 + C14H28, where carbons 3 + 14 = 17 and hydrogens 8 + 28 = 36 balance perfectly, so this is likely.
options.B: C4H8 is a valid alkene product. Cracking could give C4H8 + C13H28, where carbons 4 + 13 = 17 and hydrogens 8 + 28 = 36 balance perfectly, so this is likely.
options.C: C8H16 is a valid alkene product. Cracking could give C8H16 + C9H20, where carbons 8 + 9 = 17 and hydrogens 16 + 20 = 36 balance perfectly, so this is a very typical cracking split.
options.D: C16H34 is an alkane almost as long as the starting material. Its formation would require a C1 partner with only 2 hydrogens, CH2, which is not a stable alkane, alkene or hydrogen product. It also defeats the purpose of cracking to make much smaller molecules, so it is least likely.
